title: STEDiff: Revealing Spatial and Temporal Redundancy in Backdoor Attacks
one_liner: Backdoor attacks on image-generation models hide a lot of redundant work, and you can spot them by measuring where and when the poison actually changes the model's weights.
lead: Backdoor attacks sneak hidden behaviors into models using a trigger pattern: show the model a secret signal, and it obeys a malicious instruction. These attacks normally require hours of computation and massive memory. This paper reveals why attacks waste so much effort: certain weights do most of the work (spatial redundancy), and only a few time steps in the diffusion process matter (temporal redundancy). Using this, the paper builds a faster attack (15x speedup) and a detector that catches poisoned models by watching for the telltale weight signature.

paras: A diffusion model learns to turn noise into images by denoising step by step. An attacker adds poison during training: show the model a trigger image, then nudge it to output a malicious target. The attacker has to repeat this nudge thousands of times while the model denoises through hundreds of time steps, making the attack expensive and slow. A naive attacker tries the same poison move at every time step and trains the whole model, wasting computation.
The attacker faces two problems: the update burden (training takes too long and uses too much memory) and the detection problem (how do we even know the model was poisoned after the fact?).

callout.html: The paper finds that backdoor attacks do redundant work in space (specific weights get altered much more than others) and time (only a few diffusion time steps actually need poisoning).

steps.text: Track how much each weight changes under poison vs normal training.
Certain weights accumulate abnormally large updates during backdoor injection.
Test which time steps in the diffusion process are actually needed for the attack.
Speed up the attack by using only critical time steps and hot weights.
Catch poisoned models by checking weights for the enrichment signature.

paras: Instead of poisoning the model uniformly at every time step, the paper targets only the weights that matter most and only the diffusion time steps where the poison actually takes root.

hidden.h2: The enrichment phenomenon: abnormal update concentration
hidden.name: update concentration in critical weights
paras: When an attacker poisons a diffusion model, the nudges used to steer the model toward the attack goal do not spread evenly across all weights. Instead, they pile up abnormally in a small set of weight pairs. This is the enrichment phenomenon: certain weights are hit with massive changes while others barely move. It is not that the attacker chooses this; it emerges naturally because those weights are most influential for the attack.

The paper measures this by computing how much each weight diverges between a normal model and a poisoned one. The paper also observes that across the 1000 diffusion time steps, only a small window (roughly steps 200-600 in a 1000-step schedule) drives the bulk of the weight changes. This temporal concentration allows the attacker to skip redundant time steps, because early steps are too noisy to fully soak up the poison, and late steps are already committed to a direction and resist steering.

heat.caption: Darker weights show more update concentration during poison injection.

reads.html: The attacker accidentally exposes itself by overloading a few specific weights.
Spatial and temporal heterogeneity in weight changes during backdoor injection creates a measurable signature.

mechanism.h2: Why spatial and temporal redundancy exists
paras: Diffusion models work by reversing a noise-to-image process at each time step. Only certain weights are sensitive enough to steer the final output toward the attack target. The attacker's updates converge on these few critical weights, creating the enrichment phenomenon. If you try to poison less-influential weights, the model washes out the change during the next denoising step, wasting computation.

Temporally, the diffusion schedule has a bottleneck: the middle and earlier steps compress the semantic content most. Poisoning late steps (when the image is almost done) has little effect because the model has already committed to a direction. The attacker gets the most effect per step in the narrow temporal window where the model is still flexible but has enough structure to be steered. This is why backdoors can succeed using only 10-20 percent of the original time steps.

stages.s: poison update signal computed from trigger and target
most weight updates have no effect (washed out)
critical weights accumulate updates, creating enrichment
late diffusion steps are insensitive to backdoor steering
attack succeeds; detector sees the weight signature

math.words: The gradient concentration at weight i during poison injection is: G_i = sum over time steps of how much weight i moves. Weights are flagged as critical if G_i is far higher than the median. Temporal redundancy is: for each time step, measure average weight movement; only keep steps where movement exceeds a threshold.
math.equation: enrichment_score_i = sum_t (|theta_i(t+1) - theta_i(t)| during_poison) / sum_t (|theta_i(t+1) - theta_i(t)| during_normal)
symbols: value of weight i after time step t
when the model is being attacked
when the model trains normally without attack
ratio of change during poison vs normal (high means critical weight)
add up over all diffusion time steps

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Weight w1 (normal training over 10 steps): moves 0.1+0.05+0.08+0.06+0.12+0.04+0.07+0.03+0.09+0.06 = 0.81 total
Weight w1 (same 10 steps, under backdoor): moves 1.2+0.9+1.8+2.1+1.6+0.3+0.2+0.1+0.05+0.05 = 8.35 total
Enrichment score for w1: 8.35 / 0.81 = 10.3, meaning this weight is hit 10x harder by the backdoor than normal training.

math.note: When a weight's enrichment score is unusually high, it signals the weight was the attacker's target.

charts.title: Naive attack (all time steps, all weights)
charts.note: Slow and memory-hungry but does succeed.

charts.title: STEBA (this paper: critical steps and weights only)
charts.note: 15x faster because only critical time steps run (fewer diffusion loops); 82% less memory because only hot weights are trained; success stays high because these weights and time steps do all the real work.

charts.title: STEDF detector
charts.note: Catches poisoned models by analyzing the enrichment signature in weights.

items.html: If an attacker knows the detection rule, they could try to spread the poison evenly across many weights to hide the enrichment. The paper does not test this adaptive scenario.
The enrichment window and critical time steps may shift across different diffusion model designs. The paper tests on one architecture family.

items.b: Weak trigger patterns may not show strong enrichment.
items.html: Simple or short triggers might poison the model so gradually that the signature is faint.

items.b: This paper shines when the backdoor is strong.
items.html: Clear trigger-target pairs create obvious enrichment and are easy to detect. The detection is reliable under the paper's threat model.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Train two diffusion models on a small dataset (e.g., 1000 images): one normally and one with a backdoor (use a simple trigger, like a small patch in the corner, and a clear target, like changing red objects to blue). Measure the time and GPU memory used by the naive attack and the STEBA attack. Run the STEDF detector on both models' final weights and verify it flags the poisoned one.
demo.metric_eq: speedup = time_naive / time_STEBA; memory_saved = 1 - (mem_STEBA / mem_naive); detection_rate = (models_detected / total_poisoned) * 100
demo.closing: The key observation: poisoned models show a clear, measurable signature in their weights that detection can catch in seconds.
